title: From Link Availability to Deadline-Constrained Key Service: A Feasibility Framework for Mobile Free-Space Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Mobile free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) links can provide secret bits intermittently, whereas applications may need cryptographic key material at specified times. Optical feasibility, positive finite-key output, and deadline-compliant key service are consequently different claims. This technical note formalizes their separation through a time-indexed, security-qualified arrival process and a key-inventory model. Under explicitly stated assumptions, an elementary prefix-feasibility condition characterizes whether all demands can be served without borrowing keys from future contact windows. A stylized finite block model then illustrates why positive long-run optical availability does not ensure positive finite-key output when observations are fragmented into short contacts. Two transparent numerical examples distinguish total key yield from key delivery time and show the conditional benefit of pooling data across acquisition windows. The analysis is intended as a systems-level accounting and benchmarking framework, not a new QKD security proof or a demonstration of hardware performance. It identifies measurements and security assumptions needed to evaluate train, UAV, high-altitude-platform, and satellite-assisted optical QKD against application-level service requirements.
summary: This technical note develops a feasibility framework for mobile Free-Space QKD, moving beyond simple total key counts to address time-constrained service requirements. By modeling key material in a time-indexed inventory, it establishes a prefix-feasibility criterion that determines if key demands can be met at specific deadlines. This is vital for benchmarking real-world quantum communication systems like those on trains or satellites.
main_problem: The paper distinguishes between three concepts for mobile Free-Space Quantum Key Distribution (QKD): physical link availability, guaranteed finite key output, and meeting specific application deadlines.
main_result: A prefix-feasibility criterion was established, showing that service failure can occur even if the total key supply meets the total demand, emphasizing the critical role of timing and inventory management.
method: The authors developed a time-indexed, security-qualified arrival process and a key-inventory model to track key material over discrete time slots.
model_or_system: The system modeled is mobile Free-Space Optical (FSO) QKD links (e.g., train, UAV, satellite-assisted). The model uses a key-inventory recurrence relation ($B_t = B_{t-1} + A_t - D_t$) to track key material.
key_observables: Key inventory ($B_t$), usable key arrival ($A_t$), application key demand ($D_t$), and the deficit diagnostic ($\Gamma$).
important_parameters: Time index $T$, initial inventory $B_0$, and the required prefix $u$ for feasibility checks.
main_assumptions: Assumes unlimited storage, no key expiration, and that the analysis is a systems-level accounting framework, not a security proof.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the sequence of analysis gates (Physical $ightarrow$ Security $ightarrow$ Service). Table 2 demonstrates a service outage in a key-service ledger when demand peaks before key replenishment.
paper_structure: The paper first formalizes the separation of key concepts, then develops the time-indexed inventory model and the prefix-feasibility criterion. It uses stylized finite block models and numerical examples to illustrate the limitations of simple total-yield calculations.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, systems-level accounting framework for resource management in quantum communication, which is crucial for designing practical, deadline-aware quantum networks.
